items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.

items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.
